title: How does a zipper close a whole bag with one pull?
description: Follow the tiny teeth through a zipper’s slider, spot its three main parts, and try a quick challenge with a zip you already own.

sections.title: A little machine hiding on your pencil case
sections.html:
Closing a bag takes a second. But look closely at the zip: you are joining dozens of tiny pieces without touching each one.

A zipper closes because its teeth fit together. The sliding part guides them into place, one after another. Pull it the other way and it separates them again.

The teeth are also called elements. They stay attached to two strips of fabric. YKK’s explanation of zipper construction shows how the pieces work together.

sections.title: Find these three parts
sections.html:
Take a look at a zip on a bag or jacket. This little map will help you name what you see.

The parts to look for on a zipper
PartWhere to lookWhat it does
Teeth, or elementsThe rows beside the openingFit together to close the gap
SliderThe small body behind the tab you pullGuides the teeth together or apart
TapeThe fabric strip on each sideCarries the row of teeth

The pull tab is your handle; it is not the whole slider. You can see both parts labelled in YKK’s zipper manual (page 1).

sections.title: Inside the slider is a tiny Y-shaped passage
sections.html:
Picture the letter Y: two arms meet at one stem. Inside the slider, a passage with that shape guides two separate rows into one joined chain.

  1. As you close the zip, the separate rows enter the wide end.
  2. The passage brings them together so the teeth fit together.
  3. The joined teeth come out at the narrow end.

Opening reverses the trip. One joined chain becomes two rows. The slider controls the movement; the teeth do the holding.

sections.title: The clever bit is in the shape
sections.html:
A row of smooth beads would not do the same job. The pieces need shapes that engage with their neighbours.

In Gideon Sundback’s 1917 fastener patent, each tooth has a little hollow on one side and a raised bump on the other. A bump fits into a neighbouring hollow, helping the pieces hold together. The patent describes a sliding device that connects or separates the rows.

It is a lovely design question: how can something hold together, yet come apart when you want it to? A zip answers it with carefully shaped pieces and a guide.

sections.title: Some zips have a hidden brake, too
sections.html:
The teeth fitting together and the slider staying put are two different jobs.

Some sliders include a small locking pin that catches on the teeth. Moving the pull tab releases it. Other locking sliders release when you gently pull the tab, so the details vary. YKK shows both locking designs.

That is why a zip can move smoothly in your hand but stay where you leave it.

sections.title: Try a ten-second zipper challenge
sections.html:
Use an ordinary bag zip that moves freely. Open it halfway, then slowly close a short section. Watch just beside the slider. Stop if fabric catches; there is no need to force it.

Which part travels along the opening: the teeth or the slider? Make your choice before revealing the answer.

Show me what to look for

The slider travels along the opening. The teeth remain on their fabric strips, joining as the slider passes. Reverse your hand’s movement and watch the joined section become two rows again.

Now compare it with the fastener inspired by a burr. Both let you open and close something repeatedly, but they solve the problem in different ways.

Another tiny part doing a big job: the ball inside a ballpoint pen. Your pencil case is full of small inventions worth a closer look.
